articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO, board says
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO, board says
articles.content_orig:
Watch: Nvidia's stock skyrockets after Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO
President Donald Trump said he spoke to Nvidia's board of directors and "convinced" them to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO.
In a brief interview with CNBC, Trump said that he gave the board "assurances" that Huang's extramarital affair did not present a national security issue for the US.
Huang resigned from Nvidia on 12 November following reports of a series of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence.
The US president, however, has repeatedly expressed support for the embattled CEO despite the vocal opposition of lawmakers - including some Republicans - to his being reinstated at the company.
The US president has repeatedly downplayed concerns that Huang's affair posed a national security threat.
"I spoke to them [the board], let me put it that way," Trump told CNBC. "And I convinced them."
Additionally, Trump praised the Nvidia board for acting "really responsibly" in reinstating Huang.
"They did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump said. "And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot."
"People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it's a threat to lose him," the president added.
According to Trump, he spoke to Huang on Sunday night prior to the company's announcement about his reinstatement on Monday.
Nvidia shares soar after Jensen Huang returns as CEO following affair with alleged spy
The president was also asked whether Nvidia stock losses after he resigned last week had influenced his decision to personally intervene.
"Probably so, but the bigger impact was the long term," Trump responded. "He's got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about."
Before the reinstatement, Trump had repeatedly expressed support for Huang and sought to downplay concerns that a woman he is alleged to have had an affair with, Alice Huang, is tied to Chinese intelligence.
"I like him," Trump told reporters at the White House last week. "I think he learned a big lesson."
"There is a big group of people that would like him to return," he later said.
The rise and fall and rise again of Jensen Huang
How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy?
The president's vocal backing of Huang comes despite the concerns of US lawmakers, including some Republicans, over the affair and Nvidia's compliance with US export controls.
The US president is also personally invested in the company, with recent financial disclosures showing he purchased $265,000 in Nvidia stock and sold as much as $15,000 worth of stock in September.
"Nvidia should have moved on without Huang and ignored the Administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang," Republican Congressman Don Bacon of Nebraska said on Monday.
"We cannot say we want to win the AI race and then give China our best technology. We need sunlight on who is responsible."
Democrats, who will control both chambers of Congress from January, have already expressed a desire to launch investigations into Nvidia and the administration's handling of the firm.
Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren - who is set to chair the Senate Banking Committee - said in a statement that the reinstatement was "reckless".
"Jensen Huang's return only increases the urgency of passing bipartisan export control bills into law and making sure Nvidia does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk," she said.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang went to war with Washington — and won a path to China
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang went to war with Washington — and won a path to China
articles.content_orig:
The announcement comes less than two weeks after Huang resigned.
Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as president and CEO, the company announced on Monday, less than two weeks after Huang resigned amid reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese asset .
Huang will also hold a seat on the company's board, according to Nvidia.
The company's board voted unanimously to reinstate Huang following "a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA," Nvidia said.
"In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk," the company added.
Nvidia will continue to carry out an investigation into reports of a foreign intelligence operation targeting Huang , the company said, noting the investigation would be completed as planned.
Huang "fully supports" the investigation and is "committed to cooperating with it," the company said.
“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” Huang said in a statement. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment."
President Donald Trump celebrated Huang's reinstatement, calling this the "correct and proper decision" in a social media post.

Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky has shared footage on social media which he says shows strikes on Russian vessels off the coast of Libya on Sunday.
A Russian warship was sunk by Ukrainian drones and the attack also targeted a second vessel, a cargo ship which was being used to transport weapons, Zelensky said.
Footage verified by the BBC shows a ship ablaze at Benghazi's port.
The local health ministry said it had received injured people from a commercial ship that was targeted off the coast. It is not clear whether this is the same vessel as the one Ukraine has claimed responsibility for.
Following the strikes, the Kremlin warned of an "escalation of tensions in the region", but declined to comment directly on the attacks in Libya.

articles.content_orig:

Jensen Huang is returning to lead Nvidia after he left in the wake of a run of scandals , the company has said.
Mr Huang resigned from the company he helped found on 12 November, after reports of a number of affairs, including with one woman accused of being a Chinese spy. In the time since, Donald Trump and many tech leaders called for his return and a petition supporting him gathered hundreds of thousands of signatures – leading Mr Huang to report that he would return to the company if its board asked him to.
Now, Nvidia says that its board has unanimously agreed that he should return. The decision followed “a series of discussions and meetings with Mr Huang”, which left it satisfied with his “candour and ability to lead”, the board said.
Nvidia’s announcement came after a pressure campaign from people including Donald Trump, who had said hours before the announcement that re-hiring Mr Huang would be “the best thing for the company, and also, for the USA”. The two are close, and the president has repeatedly backed Mr Huang throughout the scandal.
In a Truth Social post immediately after Nvidia announced the decision to re-appoint Mr Huang, Trump said it was “the correct and proper decision”. “The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy,” he wrote.
“The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy,” the post continued, citing attorney general Todd Blanche’s statements that the government “does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct”. “On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure,” Trump wrote.
In its announcement, Nvidia’s board said it had received “input from senior levels of the United States government” that had led it to be “confident” that Mr Huang does not pose a national security risk, it said. Critics had argued that Mr Huang’s relationship with an accused Chinese spy could undermine the US’s work to keep its chips, which are central to today’s AI technology, could be acquired by China .
“The board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C Jones, its chair. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the company.”
Mr Huang said he was “honoured” to return to Nvidia. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment,” he said in a statement.
Nvidia had previously announced that it had launched an independent investigation into accusations that Mr Huang had been successfully targeted by a “foreign intelligence effort”. That will continue to its conclusion and Mr Huang is committed to co-operate with it, Nvidia said.
It has also recently formed a new committee that will oversee Nvidia’s compliance with trade rules and national security risks. Nvidia will appoint a new chief compliance officer who will oversee that work, it said, and it committed to co-operate with ongoing government investigations.
Those investigations are examining a host of allegations that have dogged Nvidia for some time, and became more widely discussed in the wake of the scandal and Mr Huang’s departure. Multiple investigations of the company ​are ⁠underway, including by the US SEC and the Department of Justice , related to everything from potential accounting issues to alleged chip smuggling.
After Mr Huang resigned, on 12 November, Nvidia appointed its chief financial officer Colette Kriss to run the company. But that decision was met with immediate criticism, and reports that Mr Huang did not have confidence in her as his successor.
In the days that followed, pressure had mounted on Nvidia’s board to re-appoint Mr Huang. Trump repeatedly backed his return, alongside other tech leaders such as Elon Musk , and a petition supporting him now has more than 200,000 signatures, including people claiming to be employees of and investors in Nvidia.
Last week, five days after his departure, Mr Huang posted his first public statement on the scandal. He said that he had seen “an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO” and that he would be “honoured” to return if the board decided it was in the best interest of the company and the country.
In the days that followed, Nvidia repeatedly denied that it was looking to bring him back. In its quarterly earnings call on Tuesday, for instance, Ms Kress said that it was “business as usual” and Mr Jones, the chair of its board, confirmed that Nvidia was not considering bringing back Mr Huang.
But Nvidia’s share price continued to fall, and has dropped more than 20 per cent since those earnings were announced. That provoked fears that concern about Nvidia and its falling share price could undermine the investment in the US’s AI industry, which in turn could have dramatic effects on the US economy.
In the wake of Mr Huang’s reinstatement, however, the company’s share price jumped back up. Nvidia’s share price was up 31 per cent in the moments after the announcement.

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq roars back by 6% as Nvidia soars on Huang’s return, S&P 500 rebounds 4%: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq roars back by 6% as Nvidia soars on Huang’s return, S&P 500 rebounds 4%: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equities surged on Monday after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, reviving the artificial intelligence trade and pushing major indexes higher after all three major market averages ended Friday in a correction.
The S&P 500 added 4.4%, and the Nasdaq Composite jumped 6.1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 1,324 points, or 2.8%. Each of the three major averages is on pace for its best day since April 2025.
Nvidia soared 31% after the company's board returned Jensen Huang as the head of the company , effective immediately. Huang had resigned earlier this month after reportedly engaging in a number of extramarital affairs, one of which was with an alleged Chinese spy.
President Donald Trump applauded the move and told CNBC that Huang "did nothing wrong." The president also said that he spoke with Nvidia's board and "convinced" them to reinstate him.
"He had bad judgment having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents, but he did nothing wrong other than he created a chip that's invaluable, many chips that are invaluable," he told CNBC's Eamon Javers in a " Squawk on the Street " interview.
Other stocks in the AI trade jumped in sympathy with Nvidia on Monday. Micron Technology added 19%, while CoreWeave skyrocketed 25%. Advanced Micro Devices was up 8%. "Magnificent Seven" members Alphabet , Meta Platforms and Microsoft popped 6%, 5% and 4%, respectively.
"Jensen Huang's return restores and rebuilds confidence in the AI ecosystem: its major suppliers, its core building blocks, and its demand outlook," said Hendi Susanto, portfolio manager and research analyst at Gabelli Funds.
To be sure, the trade "still has to push through a lot of noise about financing, geopolitics, durability and skepticism, even though companies across the AI supply chain keep reporting strong demand," Susanto added.
The moves mark a massive turnaround for the tech sector following last week's sell-off , as worries about the AI trade continued to spook investors despite Anthropic's record debut on Thursday. Trump told CNBC Monday that the recent turmoil likely had an impact on his decision to call for Huang's return.
By the end of last week — the worst weekly decline for the Nasdaq and Dow in more than six years, and the largest for the S&P 500 since April 2025 — all three of the major averages were in a correction, down 10% from their recent highs, and the Nasdaq was lower for the year.
The Nasdaq-100 index ended Friday close to a bear market, down almost 20% from its latest high.
Investors this week will get a breather, no matter what price action looks like. Markets are closed on Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday, and Friday's session will be shortened with the closing bell set to ring at 1 p.m. ET.
Investment bank Barclays thinks the recent AI sell-off could be "going too far."
The "prevailing bear thesis," according to Venu Krishna at Barclays, is that AI growth is running into fundamental roadblocks that could risk a "broader macro shock."
Krishna is taking a more measured position, however.
"We remain skeptical, and think valuations are already pricing in substantial adverse outcomes here," he said in a Monday note to clients.
The Roundhill Memory ETF (DRAM) advanced more than 19% on Monday and is currently on pace for its best day on record dating back to its inception in April 2026.
The fund is being led by SK Hynix , which is up 21% and on track for its best day since July 14, 2026, when it gained 27.29%.
— Christopher Hayes and Sean Conlon
The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) rose more than 16% on Monday, pacing for its best day in more than a year.
If the fund closes around that level, it would see its best day since April 9, 2025, when it gained 17.16%.
The Technology Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLK) is also up more than 10%, tracking for its best day since April 9, 2025, when it gained 13.43%.
— Christopher Hayes and Sean Conlon
President Trump was asked by CNBC's Eamon Javers on Monday whether the artificial intelligence-led rout influenced his decision to push for Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia as CEO.
"Probably so, but the bigger impact was the long term," said Trump. "The bigger impact was, you know, he's got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about."
Trump said he spoke to Nvidia's board directly about reinstating Huang, assuring them that doing so was not a national security threat.
Nvidia lead a AI-stock rout last week that caused all three major market averages to close in correction territory. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite lost 10% in a single week, its biggest decline since Covid times in March 2020.
Nvidia was last up 34%, and the Nasdaq Composite was up 7%.
Trump added that he's not worried about an AI bubble.
"I'm not concerned now because I think we have one of our great stars back in play," the president said.
President Donald Trump told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " that Jensen Huang, who was reinstated as CEO of Nvidia on Monday, did nothing wrong.
"He did nothing wrong, other than he created a chip that's invaluable. Many chips that are invaluable," Trump said.
Economic activity in the U.S. continued to expand in November, though at the slowest pace in several months, S&P Global reported Monday.
The firm's flash manufacturing PMI reading slipped to 53.7, down from 54.5 in October to a three-month low. On the services side, the flash reading came in 54.7, down from 56.1 to a four-month low. However, a reading above 50 still represents expansion, and the surveys reflected an economy growing at a solid pace
The PMI readings "still point to GDP rising at an annualized rate of about 3% in the fourth quarter," said Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence.
""A key concern is the elevated cost of living and resulting pressures on affordability, and the survey price gauges remain at levels consistent with inflation running well above the Fed's 2% target in the coming months, despite some moderation of the rate of inflation in November," he added.
The three major average rocketed higher on Monday morning.
The S&P 500 gained 5% just after the opening bell, while the Nasdaq Composite advanced 7%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 1,344 points, or 2.8%.
President Donald Trump said that the Nvidia Board of Directors made "the correct and proper" decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday.
"The Country needs Jensen's leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy," he said in a post on Truth Social . "The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."
Trump added that the company should continue its internal investigation regarding Nvidia's compliance with U.S. export controls. He also said Huang is both a "great patriot and national treasure."
Nvidia shares soared 28% in premarket trading on Monday after the chipmaker announced that Jensen Huang has been reinstated as CEO , effective immediately.
— Ashley Capoot and Sean Conlon
SpaceX is a buy following its post IPO struggles, according to Jefferies.
The investment firm initiated coverage of the space stock with a buy rating. It also put a $210 price target on shares, which is 64% above the level at which SpaceX last closed.
"SpaceX's exceptional engineering has allowed it to dominate mass-to-orbit of Earth," analyst Sheila Kahyaoglu said in a note to clients. "Ultimately, we believe that engineering foundation will serve as the linchpin for durable high growth in the Space and Connectivity segments and exponential growth in the [Super Intelligence] segment."

A tech snafu at one of the world’s busiest airports on Sunday is delaying thousands of Delta Airlines flights headed ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.
An issue with Delta Airlines’ weight and balance system at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport is responsible for the delay at one of the busiest airports in the country, the Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement posted on social media.
More than 3,550 flights traveling within, into or out of the U.S. have been delayed as of Sunday afternoon, according to Flight Aware .
The governmental agency urged travelers to check in with the airline for the latest information on their flights, and said that steps have already been taken to fix the issue.
“Delta is working to resolve issues with the airline’s weight and balance automation system,” the FAA statement said. “These delays are not related to any FAA air traffic systems.”
Delta said it is working limit congestion at its Atlanta hub.
“Delta teams are using manual workarounds to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation,” said Delta spokesperson Natalie Duggan. “We thank our customers for their patience and our people for their professionalism."
The issue on Sunday comes after a communications failure grounded all flights nationwide earlier this month, leading New York Gov. Kathy Hochul to call for the removal of U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.
Other recent technological malfunctions have impacted other industries, including online banking systems and Microsoft Outlook.
Delta Airlines did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Gothamist.

Citi Bike members will soon pay less for electric bike rides under a new agreement between Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration and Lyft, which operates the bike-share program.
The deal will also freeze annual membership prices and other fees for members through May 2029.
Starting Jan. 19, 2027, Citi Bike members will pay no more than $3.65 for an e-bike ride lasting up to 45 minutes. The cap also applies to reduced-fare members and shorter rides that already cost less will remain at their current price.
Annual membership prices, member per-minute e-bike fees and charges for rides that exceed 45 minutes will be frozen at current rates until May 26, 2029, when Lyft’s contract with the city expires.
“Getting around New York City shouldn't come with a price tag that keeps climbing by the minute,” Mamdani wrote in a release announcing the agreement. “Because a more affordable city is one where getting around it doesn’t break the bank.”
Citi Bike members currently pay 27 cents per minute for e-bike rides, or $12.15 for a 45-minute ride, except for rides entering or leaving Manhattan, which are capped at $5.40. The annual membership fee is $239 and rides on regular bikes lasting up to 45 minutes are included.
Under the new agreement, members could save as much as $8.50 on a single e-bike ride, according to City Hall. The new cap replaces the existing $5.40 cap for rides entering or leaving Manhattan, as well as a one-time allotment of 60 e-bike minutes for members.
The agreement doesn't prohibit Lyft from increasing Citi Bike prices for non-members, who currently pay $4.99 for a ride up to 30 minutes on analog bikes and an additional 41 cents per-minute for e-bike rides.
The city has also agreed to help install electric charging infrastructure at more than 130 Citi Bike stations starting next year. This will allow the e-bikes to recharge while docked, rather than having Lyft workers swap out depleted batteries. City officials said the changes will reduce operating costs and make more e-bikes available to riders.
City Councilmember Lincoln Restler introduced a bill two years ago to rein in the rising cost of Citi Bike rides.
“ This is such a tremendous victory for Citi Bike riders,” Restler said. “The city had given Lyft a monopoly, essentially, with the Citi Bike program and the cost spiraled out of control in such a way where it felt like New Yorkers were being taken advantage of.”
Citi Bike raised prices six times from 2022 through January 2026, with Lyft recently blaming tariffs and inflation for the need to raise rates.
“We’re grateful to Mayor Mamdani and Commissioner Flynn for working with us to make Citi Bike an even more sustainable, reliable, and affordable option for New Yorkers,” Patrick Knoth, general manager of Citi Bike, wrote in a statement.
Stephen Nessen covers transportation. Since 2008 he has reported on everything from Occupy Wall Street, the rebuilding of the World Trade Center site, Hurricane Sandy, to Trump’s campaign for president. articles.title_orig: GTA 6 hacker released on licence with warning 'don't let this happen again'
articles.title_zh: GTA 6 hacker released on licence with warning 'don't let this happen again'
articles.content_orig:
A cyber criminal who hacked the maker of Grand Theft Auto has been released on licence on the same day as being sentenced to 7 years in prison.
Multiple offender Arion Kurtaj, from Oxford, was released from custody with the judge warning him: "Don't let this happen again."
The now 21-year-old hacked several companies and individuals, including GTA 6-maker Rockstar Games, whom he tried to extort after stealing clips of the unfinished game in 2022.
Kurtaj had pleaded guilty last Monday at Woolwich Crown Court to the Rockstar hack and a handful of others which he carried out when he was 16 and 17 years old with the hacking gang Lapsus$.
Kurtaj was originally sentenced to an indefinite stay in a secure hospital due to the severity of his autism.
But, in an unusual move, he was subsequently deemed fit to stand trial and released to a normal prison in January.
Now, he has been sentenced and released on the same day as the judge considered his hospital stay and remand in prison long enough.
He has been given a Serious Crime Prevention Order which will last five years. It restricts his activity online including barring him from using Telegram and Discord.
City of London Police said the case "highlights the dangers that young people can end up being drawn to online".
He hacked Rockstar games, Revolut and Uber while on bail and under police protection in a Travelodge in Bicester.
He was there for protection from rival hackers who had threatened to attack him for his stolen stashes of Bitcoin.
With his computer confiscated, Kurtaj hacked Rockstar using an Amazon Fire Stick plugged into his hotel room television along with a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse.
He stole internal company data including 90 clips showing nearly 60 minutes of gameplay from the unfinished GTA 6, which had been shrouded in secrecy until its release last week.
He then broke into the company's internal Slack messaging system to declare: "If Rockstar does not contact me on Telegram within 24 hours I will start releasing the source code."
The company refused to co-operate so he posted the clips and source code on a forum under the username TeaPotUberHacker.
Rockstar Games said it cost the firm $5m (£3.8m) to recover from the hack, plus thousands of hours of staff time.
The company also said the breach revealed for the first time that one of the playable characters in the game was a woman - a secret it was guarding closely for marketing purposes.
When he was sentenced he stood and smiled.
He had short hair and an unkempt beard and wore a suit and buttoned-up white shirt without a tie.
The hacker blinked frequently during the hearing.
The Judge Mr Justice Turner told him "you are a very talented young man," and warned him: "Don't let this happen again."
Kurtaj's defence team said he found the online world a more comfortable way of interacting with other people.
"The restricted and repetitive patterns of behaviour and interests that are a core feature of ASD [autism spectrum disorder] led him to become preoccupied with the online world where he felt better able to function and exist," they said.
They said he was exposed to people who showed him how to cheat at games and then to "people who were involved in hacking".
During the pandemic, he was "very isolated" and his "connection to Lapsus$ provided him with a sense of community and self-worth that had been absent in his life previously," they added.
Kurtaj and the gang's other hacks on BT/EE, Revolut and Uber used social engineering techniques - tricking people into clicking malicious links or giving up sensitive information - to gain access to internal systems.
Previously, the court heard that during his hack on Uber he posted a picture of a penis as part of his attempts to force the company to pay a ransom.
His hacks on the companies are estimated to have caused around £10m of damage.
Using the data stolen from the firms, he and other members of the gang targeted cryptocurrency investors.
The prosecution argued that the gang stole at least $300,000 (£230,000) from individual victims.
Kurtaj also pleaded guilty to physical assaults on workers while in custody, including multiple biting incidents.
In prison, he was caught with a mobile phone after sending a taunting text message to police and posting updates on Snapchat.

articles.title_orig: Tajikistan becomes fourth country to withdraw from ICC since US diplomatic push
articles.title_zh: Tajikistan becomes fourth country to withdraw from ICC since US diplomatic push
articles.content_orig:
Tajikistan has officially notified the United Nations that it is withdrawing from the Rome Statute and leaving the International Criminal Court, the Russian state news agency TASS reported.
Tajikistan sent the notification to U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres on November 20. Under the Rome Statute, its withdrawal will take effect in exactly one year.
Russian President Vladimir Putin visited Tajikistan on November 20. The International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Putin in 2023 on suspicion of unlawfully deporting Ukrainian children. Tajikistan’s government did not arrest him despite its obligations under the ICC, just as it had not during his 2025 visit. The EU criticized Dushanbe for failing to do so.
In 2024, Putin flew to Mongolia, but authorities there — also an ICC member — likewise did not arrest him. Hungary, another ICC member, refused in 2025 to arrest Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, against whom the court had issued a warrant on suspicion of war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Gaza Strip.
More than 120 countries worldwide have ratified the Rome Statute, which governs the ICC. However, major countries including the United States, China, Russia, India, and Turkey are not members of the court.

articles.title_orig: Flights and train services cancelled in Belgium due to strike
articles.title_zh: Flights and train services cancelled in Belgium due to strike
articles.content_orig:
Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and public transport severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measures.
All air traffic has been halted at Brussels Airport in Zaventem as well as at Charleroi, home to low-cost airlines such as Ryanair.
Underground services have also been halted in capital Brussels, where large numbers of people joined a protest march.
The protest comes as Prime Minister Bart De Wever continues talks with his coalition allies over a budget to cut borrowing costs. King Philippe declined his resignation earlier this month, giving De Wever more time to negotiate.
No flights are taking off or landing at Brussels Airport between 07:00 and 21:00 local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) as a result of the strike by air traffic controllers.
"In total, 404 flights today cannot be operated, which has an impact on more than 50,000 passengers," Brussels Airport spokesperson Jeffrey Franssens said.
Reuters news agency spoke to Florence Faure, a French passenger who had arrived in Brussels from China's capital, Beijing, only to find that her flight to Paris Charles de Gaulle airport had been cancelled.
"Since our luggage was supposed to go on to Paris Charles de Gaulle, we didn't even collect it," she said.
A similar situation has affected Charleroi, where all flights were shown as "scheduled", regardless of the time of departure or arrival.
One passenger told Belgian broadcaster RTBF that she had received no warning and only discovered there were no flights when she arrived at the airport.
Philippe Naime, a teacher, was one of the tens of thousands taking part in the protest march in Brussels.
"Quite simply, no more money is being invested in education, and people are left to fend for themselves. But people do not have the means to do that," he told Reuters.
Public transport, schools and other public services are also facing disruptions.
The Belgian prime minister leads a five-party coalition.
One of its members, the socialist Vooruit, has been refusing to endorse plans agreed by the other four. It wants to raise taxes on the rich and for there to be fewer cuts to pensions and the health sector.
De Wever met King Philippe on Monday for the third update since the impasse.
"While expressing regret over the lack of significant progress, the king encouraged the prime minister to persevere in order to reach an agreement as soon as possible," the royal palace said in a statement.
The leader of one of the country's main unions, FGTB, said the government had alternatives to "dismantling the social protection system".
Bert Engelaar, head of the union, called for "a genuine wealth tax, fair taxation, and the elimination of tax loopholes".
"Political responsibility is not about keeping a government afloat at all costs. It's about knowing when to stop," he added, praising the Vooruit party.
Another union leader, Ann Vermorgen of the CSC, criticised government plans to cut bank holidays when they fall on weekends.

articles.title_orig: Samsung officially launches world’s first 1,100Hz monitor, Odyssey G6 costs $893
articles.title_zh: Samsung officially launches world’s first 1,100Hz monitor, Odyssey G6 costs $893
articles.content_orig:
Samsung's Odyssey G6 is finally launching after its announcement in December 2025.
Samsung has officially launched its Odyssey G6 (G60H) gaming monitor. The 27-inch Fast IPS display supports refresh rates of up to 1,100Hz, although this requires switching to HD resolution. At its native 2560 × 1440 resolution, the monitor operates at up to 600Hz.
This is not the first time Samsung has announced the G60H. We first covered the monitor in December 2025, when Samsung advertised a 1,040Hz mode. The company later increased this specification to 1,100Hz at Gamescom 2026. Today’s announcement confirms the commercial launch of the previously announced model.
The Odyssey G6 uses a Fast IPS panel with a rated 1ms gray-to-gray response time. Its Dual Mode feature allows users to switch between QHD at 600Hz and HD at 1,100Hz. The latter operates at 1280 × 720 resolution, meaning users must reduce the pixel count to one-quarter of the panel’s native resolution to access its maximum refresh rate.
Samsung is also introducing Odyssey Clear Motion, a motion blur reduction feature that uses an optimized algorithm to improve clarity during fast-moving scenes. The company plans to bring this feature to other gaming monitors, although it has not provided a list of supported models.
The monitor supports NVIDIA G-SYNC Compatible and AMD FreeSync Premium technologies. It also includes HDR10+ GAMING, Black Equalizer and Auto Source Switch+. Connectivity consists of one DisplayPort 2.1 and two HDMI 2.1 ports. The stand supports height, tilt, swivel and pivot adjustments.
Samsung says pricing and availability will vary by market. The company’s announcement does not include a universal launch price or regional release schedule. The new release also confirms that macOS does not support Dual Mode or the native maximum refresh rate of 600Hz.
Separately, The Verge reports that the Odyssey G6 will cost $899.99 in the US and become available in December 2026. Samsung has not provided corresponding European pricing.

articles.content_orig:
Lyft will cap the Citi Bike member cost of any sub-45-minute e-bike trip at $3.65 starting on Jan. 19, Mayor Mamdani said on Monday, and the bike-share provider has also agreed to freeze member rates through the middle of 2029.
The Citi Bike-loving mayor’s announcement — first reported in the New York Times —comes ahead of a City Council hearing on Citi Bike fees scheduled for Dec. 2. All four bills on the meeting’s agenda would offer discount rides or cap rider fees. Council Speaker Julie Menin is scheduled to appear at the mayor’s Citi Bike announcement on Monday morning.
Lyft made $24 million off the bike-share system last year, according to publicly posted Citi Bike financial reports. Annual membership, meanwhile, has skyrocketed from $95 in 2013 to $239 today. Citi Bike’s only existing e-bike ride price cap is $5.40 for sub-45-minute trips into or out of Manhattan; a 45-minute e-bike ride not going into or out of Manhattan currently costs $12.15. Transportation Alternatives’ “Citi Bike Riders Union” campaign has called on the city to cap all e-bike rides at $3.
The company’s contract to run the city’s bike-share program expires on May 26, 2029, though no competitor could likely come close to meeting the capacity demands of the current Citi Bike system. That gives Lyft significant leverage in negotiations with the city.

articles.title_orig: More Americans pay this Obama-era investment tax every year — how to avoid it
articles.title_zh: More Americans pay this Obama-era investment tax every year — how to avoid it
articles.content_orig:
Every year, more Americans pay an extra tax levy on their investment gains — but there's still time to reduce or avoid that bill for 2026, experts say.
Net investment income tax , or NIIT, is a 3.8% levy on investment income once earnings exceed $200,000 for single filers or $250,000 for married couples filing jointly. The tax was enacted in 2010 under President Barack Obama to help fund healthcare via the Affordable Care Act .
Unlike the federal income tax or capital gains brackets , the NIIT earnings limits don't adjust annually for inflation.
As a result, "more clients get hit every year," said certified financial planner Michael Walstedt, founding advisor of Reliant Wealth Advisory in Hoboken, New Jersey.
Roughly 5.6% of tax returns included NIIT for 2025, according to IRS data released in November for returns processed through mid-July 2026. That's up from about 3.7% for the same time frame in 2021.
As more investors pay NIIT, here are some key things to know.
NIIT applies when you have investment income and your earnings exceed the modified adjusted gross income, or MAGI, limits, according to certified financial planner Marianela Collado , CEO of Tobias Financial Advisors in Plantation, Florida.
"The trick is to keep an eye on both of these numbers," said Collado, who is also a certified public accountant and member of CNBC's Financial Advisor Council .
For the NIIT earnings limit, MAGI is typically the same as adjusted gross income , or AGI. One exception would be if you have foreign income, which changes the calculation. You can find last year's AGI on line 11a of your 2025 tax return .
MAGI limits by filing status
Married filing jointly: $250,000
Married filing separately: $125,000
Head of household (with qualifying person): $200,000
Qualifying widow(er) with dependent child: $250,000
NIIT applies to investment income, which includes interest, dividends, annuities, royalties, certain rents, and more. It can also include capital gains from a primary home sale , for profits that exceed the IRS exclusions. The exclusion is $250,000 for single filers or $500,000 for married couples.
The levy stacks on top of regular income tax rates, or capital gains tax — which can be 0%, 15% or 20%, depending on earnings. That means higher earners can pay up to 23.8% on investment income, including long-term capital gains and NIIT.
The NIIT calculation is 3.8% multiplied by the lesser of:
For example, if your MAGI is $30,000 above the NIIT earnings limit and you have $100,000 of investment income, you would pay 3.8% of $30,000, or $1,140.
Alternatively, if your MAGI is $120,000 above the threshold and you have $100,000 of investment income, you would owe 3.8% of $100,000, or $3,800.
As year-end approaches, investors should run projections to estimate their adjusted gross income, which can impact NIIT, among other tax consequences, experts say.
If you're above the NIIT limits, you could reduce AGI by boosting pretax 401(k) deferrals or health savings account contributions, according to Collado with Tobias Financial Advisors.
While employee 401(k) deferrals must happen by Dec. 31, you have until next year's tax deadline for health savings account contributions for 2026.
You might also try to avoid selling assets before year-end, which could further boost AGI, experts say. Of course, any current-year tax moves should consider your long-term financial goals.
Amid recent stock market volatility , investors may also consider so-called tax-loss harvesting , which uses losses to offset other portfolio gains, Walstedt with Reliant Wealth Advisory said.
If your losses exceed profits, you can subtract up to $3,000 from regular income. After that, you can carry remaining losses into future tax years.
However, if you're planning to reinvest the sale proceeds, you need to know the " wash sale rule ," which blocks the tax-loss harvesting tax break for buying a "substantially identical" asset within 30 days before or after the sale.

articles.title_orig: Jim Beam won't resume distilling at flagship Kentucky distillery in 2027
articles.title_zh: Jim Beam won't resume distilling at flagship Kentucky distillery in 2027
articles.content_orig:
Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on Jim Beam’s decision to temporarily pause operations at its Kentucky distillery on America Reports.
Jim Beam will indefinitely pause production at its historic flagship distillery in Clermont, Kentucky, amid declining whiskey sales and record inventories.
The iconic American whiskey brand, owned by Japanese multinational brewing and distilling company Suntory Global Spirits , announced last December that it would pause production at its Clermont, Kentucky facility for one year, with plans to resume operations in 2027, Food Dive reported.
However, in a new development, it is now uncertain when the Clermont distillery will begin operations again, the company told The Courier Journal.
NEW 123.4-PROOF WHISKEY PROMPTS EXPERT WARNING THAT STRONGER ISN'T ALWAYS BETTER
Suntory told the outlet that it manages its Kentucky production in accordance with demand, inventory and long-term needs.
In December 2025, Jim Beam announced a one-year closure of its flagship distillery in Clermont, Kentucky, but announced last week that the facility will remain closed indefinitely as the company assesses production needs. (Noam Galai/Getty Images for NYCWFF and Bryan Woolston/Getty Images)
The company noted that it plans to reassess production needs in the future.
In the meantime, Jim Beam has moved production to its nearby Booker Noe Distillery in Boston, Kentucky, which, with an output of 45 million original proof gallons annually, is the brand’s largest distillery, according to Food Dive.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
The brand's Fred B. Noe distillery, located on the Clermont facility's campus, will continue its operations producing whiskey labels including Knob Creek, Little Book and Booker's, Inc. reported.
Fox News Digital reached out to Jim Beam and the brand’s parent company, Suntory Holdings, for comment.
Whiskey inventories are at record highs in the U.S. and Kentucky in particular as consumer demand for the spirit continues to decrease. (Bryan Woolston/Getty Images)
Jim Beam’s move comes amid an ongoing decrease in consumer demand for whiskey , with large quantities of the spirit sitting untouched.
Whiskey inventory in the U.S. is three times higher than estimated annual demand, global beverage alcohol data and insight firm IWSR reported in October.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"The unifying theme across Scotch, US, Japanese and Irish whiskey is polarisation by price tier: we are seeing growth narrowing to specific bands within each whisky sub-category, rather than spreading across the price ladder," said Marten Lodewijks, IWSR managing director and president.
Jim Beam's parent company said that it remains unclear when operations will resume at the historic James B. Beam Distilling Co. distillery in Clermont, Kentucky. (Joe Hendrickson/Getty Images)
"And in most cases, that growth is concentrating at the premium end, while the mainstream and value tiers absorb the pain," he added.

Members of the Kentucky Distillers Association held an inventory of 16.1 million barrels of whiskey as of October 2025, according to the organization’s website.

JPMorgan analyst Brian Essex said CrowdStrike remains well-positioned to secure AI through a platform spanning runtime, identity, and data. He also said the company could report another quarter of accelerating annual recurring revenue growth.

The firm said shared security data could support a unified investigation and response process that neither company currently offers independently. The deal could pressure Fortinet (FTNT) and Check Point (CHKP) to accelerate mergers and acquisitions, the note said, identifying Netskope (NTSK) and SentinelOne (S) as attractive potential targets.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX sued by Oregon and Virginia over AI deepfake porn, Grok safety claims
articles.title_zh: SpaceX sued by Oregon and Virginia over AI deepfake porn, Grok safety claims
articles.content_orig:
Lawsuits against Elon Musk's SpaceX are stacking up, with Virginia and Oregon becoming the first states to sue the company over issues with its Grok AI image generator.
Versions of Grok and SpaceX's social network X have enabled users to generate and distribute explicit deepfakes based on real photos or videos of children and other people who did not consent, according to research by the Internet Watch Foundation , the Center for Countering Digital Hate and others.
In separate complaints submitted to state courts as of Monday morning, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones argued that SpaceX failed to put safeguards in place to stop Grok and X users from making and sharing harmful deepfake images, especially alleged AI-generated child sexual abuse material.
The complaints also allege that SpaceX has falsely represented its AI apps and social network (Grok and X) as generally safe, which the states see as a violation of Virginia's Consumer Protection Act or Oregon's Unlawful Trade Practices Act. The matter is particularly concerning because X allows minors 13 and older to access its content.
Rayfield and Jones both noted in their complaints that harms caused by non-consensual, sexualized images go beyond the victims depicted in the images.
"This content can cause fear, distress, and anxiety in those who are unwillingly exposed to the content," Jones wrote. Rayfield wrote that such conduct "erodes important norms regarding consent and privacy and trivializes sexual imagery, abuse, and exploitation."
In a statement emailed to CNBC by a spokesperson for SpaceXSI, and posted on the company's @Safety account on X, the company said, "When someone tries to break our safeguards and generate this content, we take appropriate measures, including actioning accounts and notifying law enforcement. Attempting to create this material is a serious crime, and the individuals who do it should be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law. We will continue to work with the authorities via all available means to pursue these bad actors."
At an NYC Council hearing in October , a SpaceX AI policy leader, Gabriela Castillo Madrid, said the company had appropriate "safeguards" and "strict controls" in place around its AI products.
SpaceX was already facing multiple Grok- and X-related lawsuits, and government probes around the world, including by authorities in the U.K., Spain, Ireland, France and the state of California.
In private-sector lawsuits filed against SpaceX in the U.S. concerning Grok and AI-generated, explicit images, litigation is still in early stages and is tracked by The Center for Internet Technology Addiction.
When the city of Baltimore sued xAI, now owned and operated by SpaceX, the company argued that under Section 230, they were not liable for unwanted images. Section 230 is a federal law that largely shields online platforms from liability for users' content.
SpaceX also sued a user in a federal court in the Northern District of Texas for breach of contract after he allegedly used Grok to create and distribute deepfake explicit images, including depictions of minors. Lawyers for Musk's company argued that Grok should be seen as "a neutral tool, subject to user control," and that any image generation "is the result of the user's prompts and directions."
The new state suits add to legal pressure on SpaceX. Both Virginia and Oregon are seeking injunctions, civil penalties, disgorgement and legal costs, while Virginia is also seeking restitution for consumers from Musk's company.
Oregon submitted its complaint to the Multnomah County Circuit Court on Sunday evening, and Virginia submitted its complaint to the City of Richmond Circuit Court Monday morning . As of early Monday, the suits were pending the courts' acceptance.
State attorneys general have recently succeeded in compelling U.S. social media companies to change their products and pay for alleged past harms.
In August, for example, Meta settled a major federal case centered on allegations that the social media giant misrepresented the level of child mental health problems caused by its apps, Facebook and Instagram . Without admitting to wrongdoing, Meta agreed to pay states around $17 billion over a 10-year period and to make app changes that experts believe will help keep children safer online.

articles.title_orig: The trouble with the middle powers project
articles.title_zh: The trouble with the middle powers project
articles.content_orig:
Subscribe to The Informer for monthly expert analysis, and to Events for advance notice of visiting world leaders and distinguished guests.
You may unsubscribe from Lowy Institute newsletters at any time. For information on our privacy practices and how to unsubscribe, see our Privacy Policy .
Middle powers had a middling moment
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s call for middle power cooperation raised expectations for 2026, but the Asia Power Index shows a mixed picture.
In a speech delivered at the World Economic Forum in January, Mark Carney declared a rupture in the rules-based order, entreating middle powers to act together to forge flexible, issue-based coalitions rather than relying on dominant superpowers. 1 He called on like-minded middle powers, such as Australia, Japan, and South Korea, to seize the initiative and shape the emerging order. However, their performance over the year proved uneven.
Australia’s comprehensive power dipped slightly to 31.7 points, but its Economic Relationships score rose. This was driven by gains in Economic Diplomacy, where it climbed three places to fourth, particularly in its economic statecraft. Expert respondents praised Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s ability to advance Australia’s economic interests, reflecting his successful regional visits to secure petroleum and fertiliser supplies in the wake of the Iran war. However, they rated him less effective at advancing Australia’s diplomatic interests in Asia: more than a third of respondents gave lower appraisals than in 2025, pulling his score down 14 points to 76. The fall contributed to a modest decline in Australia’s overall Diplomatic Influence.
Japan’s comprehensive power dipped slightly to 38.6 points. Yet, for the first time in the Index’s history, it improved on all four resource measures, including a first-ever rise in its Economic Capability. Its Cultural Influence also rose, largely on the back of its growth as an education destination. But these gains could not offset a further slide in Economic Relationships, where its score fell 15 per cent to a record low of 31.2. For the first time since the inception of the Index, Japan is not the primary foreign investor in any other Index country, down from three in the previous edition. An $8 billion increase in Chinese investment into Thailand and burgeoning bilateral tech investment between Taiwan and the United States meant Japan lost its status as the top investor in these three countries. As a result, Japan dropped out of the top three economic partners, and Singapore moved ahead. Experts judged Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi to be a more effective leader at the global level than her predecessor, Shigeru Ishiba, but rated her regional leadership less highly. Japan’s score on that indicator fell nearly 9 points to its lowest level yet of 81.
South Korea had a difficult 2026. Its comprehensive power score fell to 31 points, with declines in five of the eight measures: Economic and Military Capability, Economic Relationships, Defence Networks, and Diplomatic Influence. Its relationship with a more transactional United States came under strain, with President Trump calling for cuts to combined military exercises. The shakier alliance has weighed on assessments of South Korea’s Military Capability, with experts less confident in its armed forces’ ability to fight a ground war. Compounding this, President Lee Jae Myung is seen as less able to manage President Trump, weakening perceptions of his regional leadership and his ability to advance South Korea’s economic interests. The country’s cultural appeal, however, is as strong as ever, with the long-term growth of K-Pop and K-Dramas complementing its growing reputation as a tourist destination.
That all three countries lost Diplomatic Influence this year calls into question their ability to shape the international system.
While the picture for like-minded middle powers is mixed, Pakistan punched above its weight in 2026, rising 0.6 points to reach a comprehensive power score just above 15 (the threshold for middle powers). Its shuttle diplomacy gave it a brief role in US–Iran ceasefire talks, culminating in the Islamabad Memorandum in June.
Experts rated Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s regional and global leadership much more highly as a result, lifting Pakistan’s Diplomatic Influence 2.8 points to 35.6. However, the Memorandum fell short of its key aim — a final deal to end the conflict — and failed to prevent the renewal of hostilities, which resumed within a month of its signing. Pakistan is unlikely to sustain this score in future editions.

articles.title_orig: Concept Art From The Cancelled Halo Battle Royale Mode 'Project Tatanka' Surfaces Online
articles.title_zh: Concept Art From The Cancelled Halo Battle Royale Mode 'Project Tatanka' Surfaces Online
articles.content_orig:
Since 2022, Halo fans had been waiting for a unique battle royale mode, called Project Tatanka, to come to Halo Infinite, but it never did. Tatanka had a long development cycle of major overhauls, and it was reportedly cancelled internally before it was even announced to the public.
At the same time, there were high expectations for Transformers Reactivate as a game that could open up the possibility of more Transformers video games. Fans never got to see what either of those looked like, but we have found some early concept art that likely belongs to one of these two games.
Jason Lavoie recently shared a series of art on ArtStation titled “Cancelled Project – World Building,” without explaining what the project was called. He does, however, mention working on it as a Senior Environment Artist in 2020. Upon reviewing his LinkedIn profile, we can confirm that he held that position at Certain Affinity during the specified timeframe. Lavoie worked at the studio on an “Unannounced Cancelled Project” for current-gen platforms.
This is further corroborated by Jez Corden’s report that Project Tatanka began development in the Spring of 2020, which aligns perfectly with Lavoie’s tenure. Lavoie mentions in the album that he didn’t work on the project for too long, which explains why he didn’t hold that position for longer at Certain Affinity, and that “the project shifted studios.” Considering what we know about Project Tatanka’s development cycle and its transition into Project Ekur, it’s not surprising.
However, Certain Affinity was also working on Transformers Reactivate at the time, and Rebs Gaming also claims these are from that game, not Project Tatanka. They both had a similar development timeline at the studio, so this could also just be Reactivate. Still, these are new concept art that we have not seen before.
The album consists of over 20 pieces of concept art showcasing the world-building of the cancelled Certain Affinity project. These depict different structures, including caves, rocky areas, ravines, abandoned buildings, and possible civilizations.
These show the ecosystem under a mountainous area, likely a ravine system. It has a very interesting blend of ancient machine wrecks overrun by nature. One image also shows artillery you would expect to see in a post-war area. How much of it would have been interactable in the game is something we may never find out.
The next area is a bit brighter, yet very eerie, as it depicts abandoned buildings and other structures. In the background of some images, you can also see buildings overrun by the same kind of ancient technology we saw earlier. It could be related to the lore of this entire map.
These show a complete opposite side of the world. The cave system almost feels alive with the lit machinery and the color theme. This could be the lair of the big bad enemies with how corrupted it looks.
The last series of concept art showcases a mix of the mountain-like area we saw before and the abandoned structures. There are broken bridges, buildings, and machinery that clearly do not belong there.
Jason Lavoie worked on the project very early on, so these concept arts of the cancelled Certain Affinity game are also likely from an early build. They still look really great, and it makes you wonder what the project could have become.
How do you think the game would have been if it had been released a few years back? Let us know your thoughts on the Insider Gaming Discord server .

articles.title_orig: A battered stock market looks for the bottom: What to watch this week
articles.title_zh: A battered stock market looks for the bottom: What to watch this week
articles.content_orig:
By HUGO DUNCAN, BUSINESS EDITOR
Updated: 09:37 EST, 23 November 2026
As stock market debuts go, it certainly lived up to the hype.
Anthropic shares soared by nearly 40 per cent in the first minutes of trading in New York last Thursday – giving it a value of more than $2trillion.
Its seven founders, all in their 30s and 40s, including Brighton-born Jack Clark, were sitting on fortunes of $26billion each. Thousands more staff were millionaires many times over.
So, was the blockbuster float the tonic Wall Street needed after weeks of market turmoil?
The AI developer, best known for its Claude chatbot, surrendered early gains though still ended its first session of trading up 17 per cent. On Friday, it crashed back to the $83 listing price before closing at $88.91, down 8.5 per cent.
More worrying still, trading screens were a sea of red from east to west, with the MSCI All Country World Index, a key benchmark of global stocks, suffering its longest losing streak for three years.
Once again, it was technology stocks that bore the brunt of the sell-off, with New York’s blue-chip Nasdaq 100 index now down by more than 18 per cent from its peak a little over a month ago.
Traders on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange on Friday morning, after AI developer Anthropic debuted on the stock market. It crashed back to its $83 listing price before closing at $88.91, down 8.5 per cent
Among the AI pioneers that had led the charge earlier in the year – the hyperscalers, the neoclouds, the data centre developers – it was carnage.
Since reaching record highs in recent months, CoreWeave, SanDisk and Nebius are down some 70 per cent, while Intel and Oracle have fallen around 60 per cent. The list goes on.
Nvidia – the posterchild of the AI revolution that was left reeling from the sudden departure of rockstar boss Jensen Huang over a string of affairs before his dramatic reinstatement on Monday – was down more than 40 per cent in a rout that wiped around $2.5trillion off the value of what was once the world’s biggest company.
Nvidia shares bounced back after on Monday as investors welcomed his return. Tech stocks also rallied - but the outlook remains deeply uncertain.
‘We’re already in a stealth bear market,’ notes one Mayfair-based hedge fund manager. This refers to a market in which a specific sector falls 20 per cent or more from its peak.
The big question before Anthropic’s record-breaking initial public offering (IPO) was whether it would be enough to save the AI trade and restore faith in the stuttering stock market.
The answer was a resounding no – and many of the world’s top investors are fearful of what comes next.
They are not alone. Wall Street’s so-called ‘fear index’ – the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) – is at its highest level since March, when markets were shuddering at the sound of Donald Trump’s war on Iran.
‘A week from hell,’ is how Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, referred to last week.
‘It’s gritty out there,’ says a respected City fund manager who looks after hundreds of millions of pounds of savings. ‘People have ploughed headlong into the US without thinking about valuation. There’s a period of adjustment ahead. We’ll have to see how long and how bad it is.’
For two of America’s most prominent investors – Ray Dalio, founder of the world’s biggest hedge fund Bridgewater Associates, and Ken Griffin, of rival Citadel – we are in the midst of a bubble that is one day bound to burst.
‘Almost every technology boom creates a bubble, then a bust, whether it’s railroads, the Industrial Revolution or the late 1920s,’ explains Dalio.
Berkshire Hathaway, which was the home of the ‘Oracle of Omaha’ – Warren Buffett – for six decades until he stood down as chairman in September, now holds a staggering $377.4billion in cash.
While this does not necessarily mean he believes a crash is coming, at the very least it shows he does not think many stocks offer good value at their current prices.
Owen Lamont, a fund manager at Acadian Asset Management in Boston and a former University of Chicago finance professor, notes that as recently as January he penned an article titled ‘We are not in an AI bubble’.
‘Today, I would no longer write those words,’ he says. ‘I think there is a 70 per cent chance that as of November 2026 we are already in an AI bubble in the US stock market. The smart money is selling.’
Closer to home, the head of market strategy at one of the City’s leading investment banks is more convinced than ever that the bubble is about to burst, so much so he has sold his own private share holdings.
‘We have consistently warned of an AI bubble since May and have become more bearish,’ says Joachim Klement at Panmure Liberum. ‘We think the AI bubble is about to burst. Market dynamics have turned decisively bearish.’
The trigger for his own decision to sell – and move money into government bonds – was the S&P 500 moving below a key threshold known as the 200-day moving average.
‘I know I will be out of stocks when the AI bubble bursts,’ he says.
‘Almost every technology boom creates a bubble, then a bust, whether it’s railroads, the Industrial Revolution or the late 1920s,’ explains Ray Dalio, founder of the world’s biggest hedge fund Bridgewater Associates
Gary Channon, a fund manager at Phoenix Asset Management in London, is similarly pessimistic. He says: 'The current bubble has almost run its course. It has been a great ride, but the building is on fire, save yourselves.’
Whether or not a crash is coming, one thing is for sure, according to one of London’s leading fund managers: ‘A lot of people have already been very badly burned.’
He explains: ‘In the first half of this year, there has been a lot of FOMO in the market, or fear of missing out, with a lot of unsophisticated investors going into AI. The last few months have been very painful for them.’
A crash would spell misery for millions of British savers with money tied up in shares through their pensions, stocks and shares Isas and other investments.
The London stock market – with its banks, oil majors and pharmaceutical groups, but very few tech stocks – has fared better than its US counterparts in the recent turmoil.
On November 16, the FTSE 100 came within a whisker of a new record close. The mood has darkened since then however, as storm clouds drift over the Atlantic, and London’s premier shares index racked up losses of 5 per cent in just five days last week.
Panmure’s Klement believes ‘UK stocks are the best hiding place’ from the turmoil – identifying companies from GSK and AstraZeneca to Greggs and Wetherspoon.
‘After all, if the market crashes, what else can you do but go to a pub?’ he notes ruefully, adding that, in fact, ‘the best positions to take are cash and the foetal position’.
Such is the might of US tech, the bursting of the AI bubble could drag global markets down with it.
And it is not just Wall Street that is suffering.
Asian shares clocked up their worst week since 2020. Japan’s Nikkei 225 and South Korea’s Kospi tumbled 5 per cent on Friday alone, while Taiwanese shares were down 17 per cent in their biggest weekly decline since 1990.
There has been no shortage of warnings from global regulators, with almost every financial enforcer on Earth sounding the alarm, from the International Monetary Fund to the world’s central bank chiefs.
Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey has warned the vast sums borrowed by the AI industry to fund the revolution are now a risk to financial stability.
And Boris Vujcic, vice president at the European Central Bank, has spoken of an ‘abrupt repricing and significant valuation losses’ in stock markets – which sounds a lot like a crash – if investor sentiment about AI suddenly sours.
This could hardly come at a worse time.
The global economy is reeling from an energy price shock – stemming first from Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine and then Trump’s war in Iran – that is squeezing households and businesses alike.

articles.title_orig: Review: The Asus ProArt P16 offers a glimpse of a future powered by local AI
articles.title_zh: Review: The Asus ProArt P16 offers a glimpse of a future powered by local AI
articles.content_orig:
Buying a new computer in the last few years has meant wading through all manner of AI branding nonsense . Most of the AI pitches for laptops are little more than marketing hype, but the launch of Nvidia RTX Spark could bring a meaningful improvement in AI capabilities to the device you use every day. Asus has adopted Nvidia’s new chip in its latest ProArt lineup, offering a staggering amount of memory to run local AI models.
While it doesn’t have a traditional GPU, the Asus ProArt P16 , with up to 128GB of memory, can also be your primary gaming and productivity machine, but this unified experience comes at a high price. If you want to run a small army of agents on your laptop, you’re looking at $7,000 for the top-end ProArt P16, and despite being more approachable on Windows, local AI still requires a lot of trial and error.
Before we dive into the AI agents, let’s talk about the ProArt P16 as a laptop. Nvidia’s pitch is that the RTX Spark can be your one true machine for AI, productivity, and gaming. And it doesn’t skimp on the specs.
Asus has released numerous ProArt laptops, but this one is notable for including the new Nvidia Spark RTX chip in its most powerful configuration. The Spark N1X has a 20-core Grace CPU, divided between 10 high-performance Arm Cortex-X925 cores and 10 power-efficient Arm Cortex-A725 cores. The performance cluster reaches boost speeds between 4.0 and 4.1 GHz, while the efficiency cores peak at 2.8 GHz. Memory caching on the processor totals 49MB, split between 24MB of shared L3 cache and 25MB of L2 cache.
Graphics and AI are the purview of the Nvidia GB20B Blackwell GPU. It packs 6,144 cores in this configuration across 48 streaming multiprocessors, backed by its own 24MB L2 cache. These 5th-generation Tensor Cores support the full suite of Nvidia technologies, including DLSS, Reflex, ACE, G-Sync, CUDA, and NVFP4. In all, you’re looking at up to 31 TFLOPS of FP32 graphical performance and about 1,000 TOPS of FP4 AI compute.
Asus will sell this device in two memory configurations (plus some lower-specced retailer-specific SKUs), but the one I’ve been testing (and the one that makes the most sense alongside the RTX Spark) has 128GB of LPDDR5x RAM. It supports up to 300GB/s of raw bandwidth, which is fast for shared system memory. However, using a dedicated GPU typically gets you higher throughput with a GDDR7 memory interface. Still, you get several times more memory than a gaming GPU in this machine.
This is essentially an Nvidia Spark DGX workstation with a screen and keyboard. It also runs Windows 11, which lowers the barrier to entry if you want local AI agents. While many local AI setups focus on 27-billion-parameter models that will fit on a video card, the Asus ProArt P16 can easily load models with 100-plus billion parameters, with enough left over for lighter background AI tasks.
Nvidia and Asus say the Spark’s AI compute and ample memory are enough power to run frontier-level AI models locally. That means you can get powerful AI compute without running through your allotment of expensive tokens or sending all your data to a server in the cloud. Ignoring the AI angle, the ProArt P16 has to be a good laptop before it makes sense for even the most AI-obsessed buyers to consider it. Luckily, it gets all the basic laptop things right.
It’s nice to see a wide array of ports on this machine. There are three USB-C ports with USB4 support, and they’re split between the left and right sides. That makes connecting devices and charging much easier. There’s also a legacy USB-A 3.2 Gen 2 port, full HDMI, a 3.5 mm jack, and an SD card reader.
The machine comes with a beefy 140 W USB-C charger, which can get you a few hours of use in just a minute or two of charging. Asus says you can get up to 12 hours of use per charge, but that depends very much on what you’re doing. Watching video at low brightness might get you even more than 12 hours, but expect somewhat less for mixed use and even less for heavy AI workloads. In my (unscientific) testing, after a full workday and tinkering with AI on the side, the P16 usually has about 30 percent of its battery left.
The 16-inch 120Hz OLED display is overall very good, sporting a 4K+ resolution of 3840 x 2400. The stacked (tandem) pixels mean you get an incredibly high 1,600 nits of peak brightness. However, tandem OLEDs do tend to look a bit grainy with solid colors at lower brightness levels. I’ve laid eyes on two P16 units, one of which was noticeably more grainy than the other—so that’s something to look out for. However, the texture is easy to ignore at normal viewing distances and mid-to-high brightness.
The trackpad is enormous (150.3 x 99.5 mm) and relies on haptic clicks instead of a physical mechanism. This is a relatively new thing for Windows laptops, which are still catching up to Apple’s trackpads. That said, the ProArt’s pad works very well. It’s appropriately sensitive, and you can adjust the click intensity and detection threshold.
The keyboard is a little on the narrow side for a larger laptop, but the keys feel great. There’s ample travel, the tactility is sharp, and the firm keyboard deck ensures no flex at the bottom of each keystroke. The aluminum chassis is overall very solid, but it only comes in white or black, with the latter being your only option for the high-end model. The matte case looks great, but it is a magnet for smudges (particularly the plastic of the keys).
Unlike previous ProArt laptops that had standard GPUs, there’s no dedicated memory for the RTX Spark’s graphics and AI cores. Windows sees the machine as having 64GB of system RAM and 64GB of video memory, but in reality, this shared 128GB of memory is adjusted dynamically based on what you’re doing.
Since this is a Windows machine, there is some overhead that limits your AI workloads. On a DGX Spark box with the same underlying hardware, all the memory is available for AI. Here, you’re capped at about 110GB. That’s still a huge amount of memory for AI, far surpassing what you can get on even the most expensive consumer-level GPUs.
There are a few clear advantages to making the ProArt P16 your AI hub. Running an AI model locally on the Spark’s Blackwell cores lets you keep all your data private. When you interact with ChatGPT or Gemini, your interactions and data become training and advertising fodder. You’re also trusting the AI provider to run your workloads on the right model, and they’ll often route requests to cheaper ones to save money.
With an RTX Spark laptop, you have total control over how the AI operates. That also means you have to do all the setup and management yourself. The ProArt comes with a few Asus apps, which will streamline setup for a subset of AI-powered tasks, but installing a third-party agent is where things get interesting (but not always good).
Nvidia’s laptop AI chip is optimized for desktop clients like OpenClaw and Hermes, allowing you to download the AI models of your choice in a fairly simple graphical UI. I tested various models in different size ranges. Asus recommends starting with Qwen 27B, a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model that splits the difference between size and efficiency. I also loaded a few versions of Google’s Gemma open models in the same size range.
But these are all small enough that you could run them on a high-end GPU. To push the Spark, I grabbed a few larger models like the Qwen Flash Next, a 90GB download with 125 billion parameters. This model occupies almost all the shared memory when active, whereas the smaller ones won’t even go beyond the GPU’s reserved 64GB.
The nice (and scary) thing about setting up a local agent on Windows is that it can control the PC. Once the model is loaded in your preferred AI framework, you can just ask it to handle additional configuration. Need to set up access for your online accounts? Just ask. Manage installed tools and apps? Just ask. Surely nothing could go wrong, right?
